A grammar, with room to grow.
Blazon describes what belongs on a shield, while leaving the drawing to the artist. This workbench uses a small, explicit English grammar and reusable vector shapes. Complex historical arms may fall outside its vocabulary.

    
BLAZON / A SMALL EXPERIMENT IN HERALDRYParsed locally. Drawn with building blocks.

  

  
LANGUAGE REFERENCE · v0.1
The anatomy of a blazon.

    
Start with the field, then add charges and their tinctures. Punctuation and capitalization are flexible. Every word must be understood before a shield is rendered.

    
Azure, a bend Or.
01 FIELD02 CHARGE03 TINCTURE

    
Tinctures

    
Fields & divisions
Solid tinctures; ermine and ermines; per pale, fess, bend, bend sinister, chevron, or saltire; quarterly with two tinctures. Patterns: barry, burely, paly, bendy, chequy, and lozengy. Use “of six” or “(6)” for pattern counts.
Per pale Argent and Azure, a fleur-de-lis counterchanged.
    
Ordinaries & charges
Counts from one to twelve. Several charges default to a balanced arrangement; “in fess”, “in pale”, “in bend”, “in chief”, “in base”, and “ill-ordered” change placement. Dexter is the viewer’s left.
Gules, on a bend Or between two mullets Argent, three crescents Sable.
    
References & composition
“Of the same”, “of the field”, and “of the first” (through tenth) refer to earlier tinctures. A final tincture may be shared: “Argent, two chevrons and a canton Gules”. “On” and “charged with” place a simple charge group on a single chief, canton, bend, fess, bar, or pale. “Between” adds a simple surrounding group.
Numbered quarterings use semicolons between groups. Each quarter contains another complete blazon:
Quarterly: 1st and 4th Azure, a fleur-de-lis Or; 2nd and 3rd Gules, a lion rampant Or.
    
Drawing conventions
Lions: rampant, passant, statant, contourné. Eagles: displayed. Trees: eradicated. Crosses: potent, pattée/patty, trefly. Chief, fess, bar, pale, and bend accept indented, wavy, or engrailed lines. Line treatments and animals are schematic; wavy and engrailed edges share a simplified contour. Armed, langued, beaked, membered, and crowned detail colours are supported on lions and eagles.

    
Current boundaries
This is a language subset, not a validator for all historical heraldry. Named arms, supporters, crests, mantling, arbitrary wing charges, semé, inescutcheons, and complex partition-specific placements are outside the grammar. Tincture-rule notices are advisory. SVGs use stylized shapes, not official emblazonments.

    
Example descriptions: Wikipedia, “Blazon”. Tests include supported descriptions and explicit rejections of complex examples.
